# SK7006 — The member nests deeper than the threshold

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

The deepest block nesting inside a member body.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Maintainability |
| Default severity | hint |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 0.8 |

## Why

Nesting depth is what cognitive complexity's nesting weight is built on, reported on its own because it is the actionable half: a body six levels deep almost always has an early return or a `continue` that flattens it, and a reader can see that from the number without reading the body. A lambda body restarts the count, because a lambda is a separate reading context.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (a) {
    while (b) {
        foreach (var x in xs) {
            if (c) {
                if (d) {
                    Use(x);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
if (!a) {
    return;
}

while (b) {
    foreach (var x in xs) {
        if (c && d) {
            Use(x);
        }
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

A metric rule has no false positives in the sense doc 16 § R3 means: it reports a measurement against a threshold, and the measurement is either right or a bug. What it can be is *useless* — a threshold low enough to fire on ordinary code teaches people to switch the category off, which is the same outcome by another route. The default is therefore set well above the corpus's p99 rather than at the textbook number, and the threshold is an .editorconfig option so a repository can tighten it deliberately. Generated code is excluded from the rule entirely; doc 07 § Metrics keeps it in the aggregate numbers, which is a separate surface.

## Configuration

- `dotnet_diagnostic.SK7006.severity`
- `dotnet_code_quality.SK7006.threshold (default 6)`
